title: The Silent Scalability Challenge: Building Live Sports Scoreboards Without Overloading the Browser
excerpt: Broadcasting live results for 13 basketball games simultaneously taught me that SSE is not just about technology - it is about respect for the client browser. How do you avoid the polling death spiral?
content:
When you are building a real-time sports scoreboard, the obvious approach is polling: every 1-2 seconds, ask "Did the score change?" Seems simple. Until you realize 13 games running simultaneously means 13 fetch calls every second, and across thousands of concurrent users, your hosting bill becomes your company's bill.

I started Scoard with that mistake. The first iteration hammered the NBA Stats API with relentless polling, and it worked - until it did not. Users complained about battery drain on mobile. The API throttled my requests. Everything felt sluggish.

## The SSE Insight

Server-Sent Events are often overlooked in favor of WebSockets, but they are perfect for one-directional broadcasting (server to client). Instead of the client asking "Did anything change?" a million times, the server says "Here is the new state when it changes."

The breakthrough: per-game SSE pollers on the backend.

Instead of one global poller that feeds all clients, I created isolated pollers per game ID. When a user opens game #1, a poller starts. When they open game #2, another poller starts. When all users close game #15, that poller dies.

Result: bandwidth scales with actual engagement, not potential engagement.

## The Fallback Strategy

Relying on the NBA CDN alone is risky - sometimes it lags. I implemented a fallback chain:

1. Try NBA CDN (fastest, usually 1-2 second latency)
2. If stale, fetch from NBA Stats API (authoritative, slower by ~3-5 seconds)
3. Broadcast whichever came back with fresh data

This hybrid approach catches edge cases where the CDN is delayed without ever serving stale data to users.

## Smart Polling Lifecycle

A game that started 6 hours ago is mostly static. Why poll for updates? The poller detects game state (finished, halftime, etc.) and:

- Game in-progress: Poll every 2 seconds
- Halftime: Poll every 30 seconds (less frequent updates expected)
- Game finished: Stop polling entirely

This simple logic reduced backend load by 60% without sacrificing user experience.

## The Lesson

Real-time architecture is not about using the fanciest tool. It is about understanding your constraints (network, bandwidth, browser battery) and matching the technology to those constraints. SSE + intelligent polling + state awareness = silent scalability.

Scoard now handles spikes of 10,000+ concurrent users during Finals week without the infrastructure of a full real-time backend. The server just knows when to talk, and when to stay quiet.

title: The ESP32 Problem: When Hardware Constraints Force You to Rethink Software
excerpt: Building SmartAgriNode taught me that when you are dealing with unreliable hardware, traditional request/response API design breaks. The solution: a global command queue that fundamentally changed how I think about distributed systems.
content:
I built SmartAgriNode with a naive assumption: HTTPClient on an ESP32 will work like a web browser. Make a request, get a response in 200ms, move on.

Reality hit hard when I realized:

- The ESP32 takes 3-5 minutes to boot
- Sensor reads sometimes time out
- The WiFi connection drops randomly
- The camera takes 10 seconds to warm up

Traditional request/response breaks under these conditions. If my backend waits for the device to respond, I either time out or lock up the entire API.

## The Command Queue Pattern

I needed to decouple the request (user clicks "Fetch Soil Data") from the execution (ESP32 actually reads the sensor).

Architecture:

1. User clicks "Get Sensor Data"
2. Backend sets: COMMAND_QUEUE['default'] = "MEASURE_SENSORS"
3. ESP32 polls /api/device/check-command every 3 seconds
4. When it sees "MEASURE_SENSORS", it reads the sensors
5. ESP32 POSTs results to /api/device/update-sensors
6. Frontend polls /api/device/sensors/latest until it gets fresh data

This pattern is nothing new - manufacturing uses it constantly. But it was a revelation in the web context: sometimes, "please do this task" is a better API design than "do this task synchronously."

## 360 Degree Field Scanning

For weed detection, the ESP32-CAM rotates 360 degrees with a stepper motor, capturing 8 images per 45 degree rotation. If the stepper jams, the entire scan breaks.

Solution: fault tolerance at every step.

Each image upload is independent:
- Image 1 uploaded -> Processing starts
- Image 2 fails to upload -> Skip and continue
- Image 3 uploaded -> Results include partial scan data
- Image 5 returns later -> Update results incrementally

Users see "7 of 8 images processed" instead of a hard failure. The system heals itself.

## Lessons for Web Developers

If you have always worked with cloud servers, hardware integration teaches humility:

1. Assume failure - Your device will disconnect. Design for it.
2. Async is non-negotiable - Your hardware is your entire bottleneck.
3. Visibility is everything - Users want to know "still scanning," not frozen UI.
4. Polling is not evil - It is a legitimate pattern for unreliable systems.

SmartAgriNode's command queue pattern now appears in every hardware integration I build. It is the dirty secret that makes IoT work.

## The Real Lesson

The best software does not fight its constraints - it designs for them. Every time I wanted to "fix" the hardware (make the ESP32 respond faster), I was solving the wrong problem. The real solution was architecture that accepted hardware reality and built around it.

That was when the system stopped feeling fragile and started feeling robust.

title: One Package to Rule Them All: How Shared Types Unified Web, Mobile, and Backend
excerpt: At NextTern, we built the same platform in three different environments: React Web, React Native Mobile, and Node.js Backend. The key to not going insane was a single shared package that every team imports.
content:
Three repos, three codebases, one problem: ensuring that when the backend defines a User, the web app and mobile app agree on what fields exist.

Duplication is the enemy of consistency. If backend User has profileUrl, but the web app thinks it is avatarUrl, you have a bug that only surfaces at runtime.

## The Traditional Trap

Most teams solve this by documentation:

"Backend engineers, please tell web that User has these fields."
"Mobile engineers, we updated the API. Here is the new contract."
[Three weeks later]
"Web still expects the old field. Spent 2 hours debugging."

Documentation fails because it is not enforced. The code does not know what the docs say.

## The Solution: Shared Types

NextTern has a /shared TypeScript package that lives in the root monorepo.

Every platform imports from @next-tern/shared:

- Backend (Express): import { User, Internship } from '@next-tern/shared'
- Web (React): import { User } from '@next-tern/shared'
- Mobile (React Native): import { User } from '@next-tern/shared'

Now when the backend team adds lastSeenAt: Date to User, both web and mobile get TypeScript errors immediately if they do not handle the new field.

No documentation. No runtime surprises. Just type safety.

## The Beauty of This Pattern

1. Single source of truth - Definition lives once
2. Enforcement - Violations are compile-time errors, not runtime bugs
3. Evolution - When contracts change, every team knows
4. Cross-platform consistency - Web and mobile behave identically because they use identical types

## The Complexity We Avoided

Without shared types, we would have implemented the same User interface three times - each with subtly different field names. avatar vs avatarUrl vs profilePicture. Subtle differences cascade into bugs. API returns avatar, but mobile expects profilePicture. Empty database, but the code compiled fine.

## The Cost of This Pattern

Shared packages are not free:

1. Complexity - One more workspace to manage
2. Publishing - Version bumping across teams
3. Breaking changes - If shared types change, all three platforms must update

For NextTern's scale (3 platforms, 2 engineers coordinating), the hassle is worth it. The guarantee of type safety across platforms is worth managing one extra package.

## When This Pattern Works

Use shared types when:
- Multiple teams share the same data models
- The codebases are tightly coupled (cannot afford runtime mismatches)
- TypeScript is your primary language

Skip it when:
- You have a single monolithic codebase
- Your APIs are public and you cannot control clients
- You are not using TypeScript

For us at NextTern, it was a no-brainer. The alternative - manual synchronization - is a maintenance nightmare waiting to happen.

title: Pages Are a Lie: How I Stopped Building Pages and Started Building Systems
excerpt: Kasparro taught me that thinking in terms of pages is limiting. When you shift to systems, you unlock reusability, consistency, and architectural clarity that pages can never provide.
content:
When I started Kasparro, I made a decision that fundamentally changed how I design products: I would never build a page directly.

Instead, every page is a composition of systems.

## The Traditional Approach

Most developers think in pages:

"Build a dashboard page"
"Build an audit page"
"Build an architecture page"

Each page owns its own state, its own components, and its own data flow. If you need the same UI pattern on two pages, you duplicate code or create a generic component that lives in a shared folder and slowly becomes unmaintainable.

This works for small projects. It breaks fast as complexity grows.

## The Systems Approach

Kasparro is built on three conscious layers:

### Layer 1: Layout Components
The skeleton of the page structure. Header, DashboardHeader, Sidebar - zero business logic. They are just containers, boring on purpose.

### Layer 2: Feature Components
The actual product. BrandSelector reads and updates BrandStore. MetricCards receives brand from store, loads dashboard.json for that brand, displays AI Visibility and E-E-A-T scores. Each feature component has a single responsibility, manages its own data loading, delegates rendering to UI primitives, and can be reused in different pages.

### Layer 3: UI Primitives
The Lego blocks from shadcn/ui. Card, Button, Badge, Select - generic, reusable, consistently styled. No state, no business logic.

## How It Comes Together

A page is just orchestration - 10 lines of code composing existing systems. The heavy lifting is in layers below. When I need to reuse MetricCards on another page, I just import it. No duplication, no component sprawl.

## The Payoff

1. Consistency - Change how a metric looks once, every page using it updates automatically.
2. Scalability - New page needed? Compose existing features. You are not starting from scratch.
3. Clarity - Developers immediately see: "This page is Header (layout) + MetricCards (feature) + Card, Button (primitives)."
4. Testing - Testing a feature component is simple: pass props, assert output.

## Why Zustand Fits This Model

I use Zustand (not Context) because the stores are the connective tissue between layers. BrandStore connects the Header (can select brand) to Feature components (consume selected brand). Stores do not contain logic. They contain state. Logic lives in components. This separation is what makes the system cohesive.

## The Bigger Lesson

Building pages is a frontend-specific illusion. Real products are built from data models, state management, feature logic, and presentation. When you design with systems in mind, pages become simple. And when pages are simple, the entire codebase becomes maintainable.

For Kasparro, this approach meant I could build 7 routes, 40+ components, and hundreds of type definitions in a way that feels coherent rather than chaotic.

Pages are a lie. Systems are the truth.
